speechtext:
The resolution will be found in the Votes and Proceedings of February 17th. It reads as follows:
Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend The Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and to provide:-
1.	(i) That the stamp tax on cheques, bills and notes, receipts for money paid by a bank, bills of exchange drawn upon persons outside of Canada according to the tenor of the bills, money orders and travellers' cheques, and post office money orders, shall on and after the first day of July, 1927, be-
Two cents in respect of each such instrument for an amount in excess of ten dollars.
(ii)	That on and after the first day of July, 1927, the stamp tax on matches shall be as follows:

On each package of matches manufactured or sold, three-fourths of one cent for each one hundred matches or fraction of one hundred
matches;
On each package containing not more than sixty and not less than thirty matches, three-eighths of one cent per package;
On each package containing less than thirty matches, three-sixteenths of one cent per package.
(iii)	That from and after the sixth day of July, 1927, the following stamp taxes be abolished, namely,-
On advances made by a bank, as imposed by paragraphs (c),	(d), and (e) of subsection
three of section twelve of the said act;
On overdrafts, as imposed by paragraphs (f) and (g) of said subsection three;
On advances by any person not being a bank, as imposed by subsection 19 of said section twelve.
2.	That the rate of consumption or sales tax be reduced to four per cent and that any enactment which may be founded on this resolution number two shall be deemed to have come into force on the eighteenth day of February, 1927, and to have applied to goods imported or taken out of warehouse on and after that date, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that date.
3.	That said section nineteen BBB be further amended by providing that, for the purposes of the said section, printers, publishers, lithographers and engravers shall be regarded as producers or manufacturers, and that any enactment which may be founded on this resolution number three shall be deemed to have come into force on the eighteenth day of February, 1927.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2.

During the debate on
the budget I called the attention of the Finance minister to a promise that was made last year by the late Minister of Customs to exempt from the operation of the sales tax small local manufacturers of sash and doors, and so forth. Under the present law, paragraph 5 provides that there shall be collected only 50 per cent of the normal tax upon the following:
Boots and shoes, including rubber footwear; biscuits of all kinds; goods enumerated in customs tariff items 86, 105 and 106: creosoted railway ties.
Under paragraph 14,-
Retail lumber dealers, who do not manufacture lumber, or who do not sell lumber to other lumber dealers, or to other licensed manufacturers, need not take out a sales tax license.
Small sawmillers, selling exclusively by retail and whose total sales are not in excess of $5,000 per year, are classed as exempt from consumption or sales tax.
Special War Revenue Act

Then, under paragraph 15,-
The following classes of small manufacturers, when selling exclusively by retail, are regarded as exempt from consumption or sales tax on the sale of their products:-Picture framers, druggists, shoemakers, upholsterers, dentists, har-nessmakers, plumbers, opticians, blacksmiths, tinsmiths, show card and sign makers.
The kind of small manufacturers that I recommended last year as entitled to exemption, and that I again recommend to the Minister of Finance, are surely just as useful and interesting as these other small industrialists, only that instead of simply sawing logs into planks and lumber, they do a little more work upon them, and sell them in a purely retail trade to the farmers and villagers around them. The late minister was so impressed with the justice of the claim that he told me he thought he could apply the exemption even under the present law, but I observe that it has not been done in the case I have in mind. The department has been demanding the tax from the small dealers to whom I referred in the budget debate some time ago. In this instance, the small local dealer, the father of twelve children, carries on, with one of his sons, a small industry; he purchases logs from the farmers and turns them into sashes and doors, which he sells to the villagers and the farmers in his neighbourhood. Out of the profits on $2,200 worth of goods which he sold in the retail trade, he supported his family and paid a salary to his son. A demand was made upon him from the government for $110 sales tax. I claim that this demand was unfair, and surely such a proceeding was not in the mind of the government when this tax was imposed. In my opinion such small industries are entitled to the same exemption as is allowed to the sawmillers who conduct business in the same way, with the only difference that the millers render less service to the small community where they operate. I am quite sure that it is sufficient to remind the minister of this matter to induce him to insert a few words in the clause, placing these small industries on the same footing as the industry to which I have referred. I was told in the department last year that they thought the present law covered those cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If I-understand the act correctly, the minister has certain discretionary powers which might enable him to do what my hon. friend desires, if he could be convinced that it was quite right and equitable. Of course my hon. friend will understand that every day, and sometimes three or four times a day, people come to the office and desire to be exempted from taxes for one reason and

another. I have just spoken to my colleague, the Minister of Customs, and we will go into this matter very carefully, and if we feel that it is right in equity, and that the law is wide enough now for us to do as my hon. friend desires, we will do it. I should not like to make any further commitment. My hon. friend will also understand that the Minister of Finance desires to obtain all the revenue he can, but I realize that in the case presented by my hon. friend of the small business such as he has referred to, the tax may be more irritable to the person concerned than it is worth to the government.

If the government and
parliament thought fit to do it in these cases, I cannot see why it should be considered a matter of favour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it is not a favour.

It should not be regarded as a favour or as an exceptional case. There are many such cases in the district of northern Quebec, northern Ontario and New Brunswick. Such small industries are essentially useful to the districts in which they are located and encourage the industrial life of the community. They complain, and quite rightly, in the province of New Brunswick that the large industry has swallowed up the smaller one. People have to build houses in the rural districts as well as in the towns or cities, and some encouragement should be given to the small local industries. If it is proper to do it in the case of the saw millers, why not give the same concession to the small manufacturers of doors and sashes? What advantage is it to the farmer, after he has had his logs sawed into lumber, if he cannot use it to put up his house or repair it? What I suggest would be simply carrying out what already appears in the law. My proposition is that the government should deal with the small industries in the same manner as they do with the large industries. If it is fair to exempt the boot and shoe industry to the extent of a fifty percentage of their sale taxes, why not exempt these small industries of a portion of their taxes, just as is done with the picture framer? I do not think the picture framer is of greater advantage to the community than the man who supplies the doors and sashes. If it be proper to exempt those industries I have referred to, why not make an exemption in the case of the manufacturer of doors and sashes? I know there are eight or ten cases of this kind in my own constituency and there are others in the northern part of the country. Why not put all the small industries on exactly the same footing?

Special War Revenue Act
The principle is exactly the same. They make use of the same raw material, purchased from the same class of people, and they render a great service to the community where they sell those produlcts at a much cheaper price than other concerns would. Jt is merely putting small, local industries of exactly the same character on an equal footing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will
not press that too far. Give us an opportunity to do something next year, after my hon. colleague has reorganized his department and looked carefully into it. In some of the cases mentioned by my hon. friend the sales tax has already been paid by the picture framer. It is just a question of where we shall draw the line. Hundreds of industries throughout the country have put up just as good a claim as my hon. friend, but we will give it careful consideration and do something later.

I have known all about
careful consideration by ministers for twenty-five years. Such consideration was promised last year by the Minister of Customs, and we know that goods kept in cold storage do not improve. It cannot be said that this is a matter which has not been 'Considered by the government and I am asking for the same application of the principle contained in the law to two industries of a like character. Why should the department favour one and demand a tax from the other? There is no reason and no justice in that. I protest against it in the name of all these small communities in those colonization regions in the northern part of the province of Quebec, extending from Timiskaming along the northern borders of the St. Lawrence valley. This is an easy way to encourage our village people to develop small local industries by making use of the raw material within the district, and it will be a practical means of preventing the exodus of our rural population to the urban centres and in turn to the United States rather than by encouraging the establishment of large manufacturing industries in our urban centres.

Last session I called the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that the owners of small portable mills doing a very moderate business in country districts had been forced to pay sales tax upon the sawing of logs for farmers. The minister then told me that there was no intention on the part of the government to collect the tax in such cases, and that if any had been collected it was a mistake. Is there any chance of these men being given a rebate for the taxes already collected?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to taxes already collected,
I must inform my hon. friend that "what we have we hold." But we will give very careful consideration to his observations.

I know that was the
promise last year, but I am informed that the owners of some of these small portable mills have been compelled to pay sales tax regardless of the extent of their business. I had a letter to this effect the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The regulations provide very
clearly that small sawmillers selling exclusively by retail and whose total sales are not in excess of $5,000 a year are to be exempt from sales tax.

The $5,000 maximum
caused the trouble. In some small communities that is not a very high figure for the year's business done by the owner of one of these small portable mills, especially where lumber is high priced, it being roughly only about $400 a month. I would suggest that if the figure were doubled it would not work a hardship to anyone and at the same time would meet with general approval.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is rather hard for me to
oppose my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and my hon. friends opposite, because I recall that when Sir Thomas White was bringing in the sales tax legislation I myself took the ground that lumber mills might be excepted from its operation. We will look carefully into this matter.

The Wx is collected on
custom work, not on lumber sawn for farmers, which is really not a product of the mill at all.

I know that the collection of the tax concerns the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler), but I draw this to my hon. friend's attention. In the community where I live it was complained in the case of a man who failed that one of the preferential claims was that of the government for sales tax. It is suggested that a better method should be devised for the collection of sales tax, and that rather than extend leniency beyond a given date it would be better for the man himself in the long run if you said, "We will not give you credit beyond that date; then you stop business or you pay." The present system involves considerable hardship on other creditors.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the Minister of Customs has that under consideration and is in agreement with my hon. friend.

At this stage I do not
want to go into the details of unpaid sales taxes, the subject having been discussed in
Special War Revenue Act

this House on more than one occasion, but it is known to the minister that many millions of dollars are in arrear, some extending over a very long period of time. This lends itself to very great abuse. Once you lay down a fixed and settled rule that if taxes are in arrear beyond a given date certain results will follow, then you attain the object you have in view. The result would be much easier for the minister, much better for the country, and in the long run exceedingly beneficial to the person in default. In response to a question from one of the hon. members for Toronto the House has before it a list of unpaid sales tax, the total running into millions of dollars. I am sure the minister will agree with me that the amount involved being so large some action should be taken to prevent a recurrence of a similar condition. Therefore I press the minister to make a declaration that this sort of thing is to be put an end to. It may be said, "some of your friends have received leniency in that regard." But that is not the question. This leniency is a distinct disadvantage to those who promptly pay their taxes, and I think the minister should take action along the lines I have suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
Two or three weeks ago I
made some comment on this matter in the House. I think every hon. member knows the difficulty we have now in collecting arrears of sales tax, but I do not think any good would result from my discussing that matter on this occasion. Let me answer my hon. friend's inquiry with regard to current taxes, which I think is what he is referring to particularly.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
Very definite instructions
have been issued that henceforth all current taxes must be collected by a certain date, and I think I may assure the committee that in future there will not be any aecretion to the present arrears.
What do you propose to do?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
One of the difficulties in the prompt collection of the sales tax has been the fact that we have had no power to charge interest on overdue payments, due to an oversight in the drafting of the original act. We have this power of collecting interest on overdue income tax. The omission is to be rectified by legislation in the present session, and I think it will be a very powerful incentive for the prompt payment of sales tax. Under the present conditions many of these defaulters
TMr. Bennett.]
have practically made the government their bankers, withholding payment of their sales tax and thus keeping the money in their business free of interest. We are making every effort to collect the arrears. Those hon. gentlemen who have been in the department know how difficult it is to put every account for arrears into the hands of the law for collection. We are doing that as far as possible, but my hon. friends will know that in all cases it is not advisable to take this course even in the interest of the government itself. However, so far as the future is concerned I can assure the House that there will not be much of an addition made to the present arrears of sales tax.
As to the question raised by my hon. friend from Labelle with regard to the exemption of certain industries, after all it is very difficult to distinguish between those who in a real sense are manufacturers and those who are not. When do we arrive at a distinct dividing line between those who merely make things in a small way and those who are manufacturers on a more or less large scale? Wre have the same difficulty in the printing trade, where the exemption from sales tax is granted to those printers who produce less than $10,000 worth of business a year. Some say that that figure is too high, that it ought to be $5,000. Here is where the practical difficulty arises. Frequently we get a protest from the man who produces $10,500 worth a year on the ground that the man who produces annually only $9,999 worth escapes the sales tax. The former says he is discriminated against. And so he is. The same difficulty arises where the exemption is put at $5,000; immediately the man whose turnover amounts to $6,000 a year complains that he is being discriminated against. I merely point out these cases to show the difficulties that confront us in the practical application of any such rule.
Within what time will the collection be made? The minister said that a certain time had been fixed.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: It will be a matter of regulation.
At the present time it is sixty days.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: The payment is supposed to be made at present by the end of the month immediately following that one in which the sale is made.

The explanation given by the minister is somewhat strange in view of what is contained in the law itself. It cannot

Special War Revenue Act
be difficult to draw a distinction between labourers on a small scale such as I have described inasmuch as there already exists that very distinction. It is no more difficult to draw the line between jobber and manufacturer engaged in the making of sashes and doors than between the man engaged in the sawmill business and the harness maker, and so on. The limitation is there in the law; it relates to those selling exclusively by retail and whose total sales are not in excess of $5,o0o per annum. That means that the manufacturer is limited in the first place as to the amount of his sales in the entire year, and secondly, as to the nature of his commercial operations. If he supplies goods to commercial houses, or if he sells more than So,000 worth per annum, he is taxed. You have two limitations there, and all I ask is that two industries which are in every respect similar, which are operated in the same manner, in the same community and which serve the same purpose, with the exception of a little more service rendered in one case, should be put on precisely the same footing If the minister is so embarrassed about exempting the small sash and door dealers, why is he not embarrassed in the case of small sawmillers? I take the law as it is; I am not suggesting anything new. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill):
That the exemption of the sales tax for small sawmillers should extend to small sash and door makers under the same limitations.
Is the resolution in-order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I was just going to call the attention of the hon. member to Sir Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, thirteenth edition, page 511. There is a paragraph of considerable length bearing on the point, but the following extract will cover it:
Nor can a member other than a minister move for the introduction of a bill framed to effect a reduction of duties, which would incidentally effect the increase of an existing duty, or the imposition of a new tax, although the aggregate amount of imposition would be diminished by the provisions of the bill.
And further on:
Nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
Under that authority the amendment moved by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) must be ruled out of order.

I would ask you, Mr. Chairman to study the point somewhat more carefully. I looked it up this morning myself with some of the authorities and I found that
so long as a private member proposing such an amendment remained within the scope of the legislation brought down by the government, and did not suggest any new tax or the substitution of one tax for another, it is competent for that member to submit any change, modification, or even increase in the application of the tax as proposed by the government. I should like to know whether the rules that apply in England apply here as well. There are hon. gentlemen who are prone to quote English precedents, and I want to retain such of them as will make for the preservation of the rights of private members. I appreciate the fact that the government should assume the responsibility for the introduction of money measures; it would be incompetent, inasmuch as it would lead to disorder, for any private member to suggest any form of taxation in substitution for another. If I proposed the imposition of a customs duty in place of this or a modification of the income tax, I can readily understand that I should be out of order. But when I merely suggest that a particular tax should be so interpreted by the government as to alleviate the burdens of a certain number of taxpayers, if I have not the right to make such a suggestion I do not know why I am here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Bourinot in the fourth edition would rather confirm the position taken by the hon. member for Labelle. But in view of the fact that he comes into conflict almost directly with the authority I have cited from May, and in view of the practice of this parliament, in cases of doubt, to be guided by British procedure, I fear I shall have to rule the amendment out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the amendment is ruled out of order, all I have to say in connection with it is that the hon. member must not be discouraged, nor suppose that we shall lose sight of his observations.

I support the views expressed by the hon. member for Labelle. It seems to me that the answer given by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Euler) is one grand argument for the income tax. Here is a man with $2,200 of a total income, paying $110 in taxes. He has no right to be taxed while we have eased the taxation 10 per cent in the case of much bigger incomes. The whole thing is a condemnation of the reduction of the income tax on the big men while we are taxing the small producer.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This section is designed to remove doubt as to the interpretation of the words "producers" and "manufacturers". A court in Quebec held that printers, publishers, lithographers and engravers were not manufacturers or producers, while the Exchequer court held that they were. This section is to remove that doubt.
Does it or does it not remove the exemption of $10,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

What is the number of the
bill?

speechtext:
It is not numbered;
it has just been read the first time and has not been distributed.

Presumably the bill will
have to be moved out of committee if it is not printed, and it will be finished at some other time. The question of the sales tax as it affects printers came before me in a very concrete way the other day when I received a letter in connection with the payment of sales tax on cases printed for the Supreme Court of Canada or the appellate division of our own court. In the one case the printer did a business of over $10,000 and the sales tax was payable, but the other party had his book printed in a small town where the printer did not do that much business and sales tax was not payable. That is a concrete case which came before me in actual business, and I do think when you deal with matters of job printing it would be very desirable to have everyone on the same basis or to raise the figure above such an insignificant amount. The figure of $10,000 represents a very limited business for a jobber in a large city, but for a man in a small village $10,000 is more than he would ever dream of doing. That is hardly fair; it is discrimination. The one man is paying large taxes, doing a large business and employing many people, while the other man is doing a smaller business and employing fewer people. I would suggest

that the amount be raised to something that would represent a real figure or that all be placed on the same basis. I mention this to the minister because it was communicated to me by an old country solicitor who had experienced it. He was very distressed because he had to pay sales tax in Calgary while another legal gentleman was not called upon to pay sales tax because his work was done in a smaller place.
Progress reported.	[DOT]

The House in committee of ways and means, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend The Income War Tax Act, 1917, to provide that the rates of tax be reduced by ten per centum.

I am not rising for the
purpose of opposing this resolution, but I desire to make a few observations in this connection since I believe it will be the only opportunity open to me of referring to a discussion which took place in this House during the session of 1926, with reference to family or personal corporations. I desire to call the attention of the government to a pledge given at that time by the then Minister of Customs, to the effect that if the law as then enacted should prove a hardship, at the very first session of parliament the government pledged itself to remove that hardship. In this connection I desire to quote the remarks of the late Minister of Customs made on June 10, 1926, and found at pages 4335 and 4336 of Hansard. The 80 per cent clause was under discussion, and in reply to some observations made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), the then minister stated:
What I am prepared to say to my hon. friend is this: We do not want to create any hardship. We do not want any concern which in reality is a partnership, which has been formed into a corporation for legitimate reasons, to suffer under the terms of this act and if any such case as that suggested at this moment as an example by my hon. friend is brought to our attention during the course of the present fiscal year, instructions will be given to the Commissioner of Taxation to withhold the levy, and at the next session of parliament this clause will be amended in a way which will meet that particular case.
I take it that that was a very definite pledge on the part of the government, and on that understanding the legislation was allowed to go through. May I call the attention of the minister to the fact that there are corporations which have been penalized by reason of the fact that the percentage is

Income War Tax Act
so high. I do not intend to go into details but I have given one particular case to the minister privately. That was the case of a corporation in which three partners owning equal shares in the business turned it into a joint-stock company for purposes of convenience only, long before the section was enacted. Two of the partners were permanent employees of the concern while the third, the president, acted in an advisory capacity only and drew no salary. Consequently that concern does not come within the law as it is at present. I submit that that is a case of very considerable hardship, and I ask the minister to be good enough to amend the law to meet cases of that kind, in accordance with the definite pledge given to the House in the words I have quoted.

Last year when the income tax proposals were before the House I called the attention of the government to the importance of encouraging the taxpayers with large families by extending the exemption of $500 for each child to the age of twenty-one years. The reasons then given apparently struck the minister as being cogent and proper, because in three or four instances the late minister, who had charge of that part of the resolution, promised that when the Income Tax Act was next amended, this would be the first amendment taken up by the government. Therefore I am quite sure that it was merely an oversight on the part of the minister when he brought down those resolutions without regard to the promise made last year by his colleague. No promise was made of a general reduction of 10 per cent of the income tax, but a definite promise was made for the further extension of the children exemption clause. It seems to me it is not necessary to develop at length the reasons. First, as everybody knows, children kept at school-and I suppose we ought to encourage parents to keep their children at school as long as they can-are more costly to their families between eighteen and twenty years of age than they are when they are youngsters. Second, twenty-one years of age is the legal age, the age of emancipation.
Oh, oh.

Yes, of legal emancipation. A child of nineteen or twenty years of age under our civil law-and I think it is the same throughout the Dominion-is not absolute master of himself until he has reached his majority. Of course, if children are earning their living, I quite admit that the exemption should not apply, but it does not apply at present. Supposing a child at sixteen 32649-77
years of age earns his living, works for himself, he does not come in under the exemption granted by law. But a child of nineteen or twenty years of age kept at school by his parents is a heavy charge upon his family, and moreover he is not considered by the government in giving exemption from taxation. It seems to me obvious from a social as well as from a sound economic point of view, that the exemption should be extended to the parents in such a situation rather than that a general exemption of 10 per cent should be granted to all taxpayers, whether they would feel the burden of paying that 10 per cent or not.
It would be quite easy to cite many concrete cases. For instance, take the father of no family with a revenue of $100,000 a year.
I have not looked this afternoon at the scale to see what he would pay, but his income tax was already largely reduced last year. He is again favoured this year by a further reduction of 10 per cent on the total amount he should pay. On the other hand, we have the father of a family of ten children earning an annual revenue of, let us say, $7,000 or $8,000. He receives an exemption for those children that are under eighteen years of age; but if he keeps two of those children at school between the ages of eighteen and twenty-one; if he wants to develop their education, if he is prepared to endure sacrifices to make them better citizens of Canada, the government disregards his sacrifices. He is struck precisely at the moment when he is making the greatest financial outlay to give a better education to his children. That is unfair, and in fact the suggestion I now make was considered so equitable last year that there was no discussion. The only reason given by the then Minister of Customs, the late Mr. Boivin, was that as the government had already made large curtailments, it was not proper to make any more that year, but that the following year, if any changes were made in the income tax, so far as he was concerned he pledged himself to see that this would be the first modification.
It is suggested that this would mean a decrease in revenue. I have already stated that the revenue derived from income taxation could be largely increased from various sources. First, this 10 per cent exemption which we are now asked to vote, could be granted only to taxpayers who have less than a certain annual revenue. I do not see why a man who has a revenue of $50,000 should receive the exemption proposed under this resolution. Surely he is not in such a position that the government is bound to take

care of him. I have suggested also that we could tax the yearly values of household property over and above a certain amount, to be determined as the reasonable rental value of the property. In that way, we could receive far more than would be compensated to fathers of families by granting that exemption from eighteen to twenty-one years of age.
Third, during the budget debate I mentioned the fact that a very large amount of revenue derived from coupons on debentures escaped taxation altogether. Last week I met in Montreal a man who deals in financial matters on a very large scale. He told me that from his experience, from the relations he had in the financial world in Montreal, he was led to believe that millions of dollars escaped taxation because of two things-that the debentures are not inscribed but are payable to bearer, and that there is no tax on the coupon. Last year I suggested that if a stamp tax were imposed on the coupons, most of which, if not all, are paid through the banks, we could increase our income tax revenue at a very small charge to the taxpayers, and thereby reach a class of taxpayers most capable of increasing their contributions to the state.
At the present time you reach easily the employee of a company because his name figures on the payroll of the company and be- . cause the list given by the manager to the income tax branch is on file to prevent that employee from defrauding the federal treasury. You reach the shareholder because companies are obliged to publish their lists of shareholders. But we do not reach one-tenth of the debenture holders because the debentures are not inscribed.

I think one-tenth would
be too large.
Mr. BOURAjSSA: Perhaps. I am not at all in that sphere of life, but I give the information as I have received it, not from opponents or partisans of any government but from business men. I give it as I had it from some of the most experienced officials of the income tax branch who tell me that they cannot and do not reach a large proportion of the biggest income of the country, an income which should 'be but which is not taxed. Surely a little attention should be given by the government to those features of the income tax, a little more added on to taxpayers capable of paying the taxation, and a little more consideration given to the father of a large family who, I repeat, is the best contributor to the development of Canada that we have. It is all very well to gather money and to pay subsidies to companies or to
fMr. Bourassa.]
charitable associations, to bring children from Europe to fill up the gaps in our country; but surely native-born Canadians are the best citizens we can have. To help fathers of families in this country to keep their children at home and to give them a proper education is far more important than to devise all sorts of plans to bring foreigners' to Canada to take the place of native sons of the land. Therefore, from a social point of view and from a sound economic point of view, I most strongly urge upon the government that they implement the promise that was made last year by one of their members. I hope the government will accept this suggestion without my being obliged to move it as an amendment, because I know that a good many of their followers in the province of Quebec at least, in endeavouring to point out to the people reasons why they should vote for the Liberal government, gave this one among others, and surely it is a good one. One of the reasons for which I upheld the government at the last session was the tendency I thought I saw in their budget proposals to come nearer to what I considered sound economics and social justice in matters of taxation, but this year I am sorry to say I do not find the same evidence. A general reduction all round of ten per cent in the income tax has been proposed without any consideration as to the means of the taxpayers and the charges that the family has to bear. That proposal is not inspired by the same spirit as was behind the proposals of last year, and if my suggestion, which I make in the most friendly spirit is accepted, it will help to correct the impression that is getting abroad that this government, after securing the favour of the people by showing itself friendly to the people, is now trying to come a little nearer to those influences that so frequently have more to do with the policy of governments-I am not speaking particulary of this or of any other government-than the real good of the people. I therefore hope that the government will accept this suggestion and implement the promise that was made last year by one of their colleagues, and upon the strength of which a large number of electors in the province of Quebec voted for the government last fall.

Before the minister replies to the hon. member for Labelle, I do not propose to allow him to get away-I am not saying this offensively at all-from the point I was trying to make in regard to these family corporations. This question has raised a good deal of difficulty and caused a good deal of distress. There was a definite pledge on the part of the late Minister of Cus-

Income War Tax Act
toms that this condition would be remedied at this session of parliament. I have already read his statement to the minister. The Minister of Customs shakes his head, so I will read it again. He said:
We do not want any concern which in reality is a partnership, which has been formed into a corporation for legitimate reasons, to suffer under the terms of this act and if any such case as that suggested at this moment as an example by my hon. friend, is brought to our attention during the course of the present fiscal year, instructions will be given to the Commissioner of Taxation to withhold the levy, and at the next session of parliament this clause will be amended in a way which will meet that particular case.
Surely that is a definite pledge. I want to tell the minister that in the case I mentioned the levy has not been withheld. I believe the commissioner takes the ground that he is only the officer administering the law, and that he is not bound by any expression of the minister on the floor of the House of Commons; I think he is quite correct in that. But here is a definite pledge that in the event of hardship being found to exist, the levy will be withheld. The levy has not been withheld, and I ask the minister to redeem the pledge of his late colleague.

I listened with great
interest to the remarks made by the hon. member for Labelle, and I was reminded of the effort that was made in 1921 by the then member for Chiambly-Vercheres, Mr. Areham-bault, to get the government to grant an exemption of $200 for each child. He was successful in this, and later the exemption was increased to $500. I also remember that a demand similar to that which is being made to-day was made upon the Minister of Finance last year, and I remember well the reply of the Minister of Customs at that time. He said that as soon as -the finances of the country would permit, the first reduction that would be made in taxation would be in that direction. I think -it is only fair, Mr. Chairman, that the father of a family of -ten or twelve children Should be granted some consideration, and should not be placed on the same footing as the father of a family that is composed of the father, the mother, and a pet dog. So I wish to approve what has been said by the hon. member for Labelle in this regard, and I would urge upon the Minister of Finance to give consideration to the suggestion that has been made.

I was just rising to say a few words in support of the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Labelle when my good friend from Quebec-Montmorency rose, and knowing his very fine record I felt 32649-774
that he had much more claim to the floor than I had. At the same time I say in all seriousness, Mr. Chairman, that I wholly agree more particularly with the earlier remarks made by the hon. member for Labelle. If we are not going to throw education into the discard entirely, if we are -going to take the attitude Which mosit reasonable people take, that education is an advantage to our children, then certainly it seems to be an extraordinary thing that a man's income should be exempted for -a certain amount only up until the time his Children reach the age for going to college, and then the exemption ceases, and he is penalized for sending them to college. I -have in mind at the moment an instance where two boys are going to the university. Up to their going to the university, the usual exemption was allowed, but now that they are at university -and their father is- put to greater expense, the income tax exemption is removed, and the father is paying a -larger tax at the very time Ms expenses, on account of these boys, are heaviest. It certainly seems a most ridiculous attitude for any of us to take to say that parents who make the effort, as most ambitious parents do, to give their children a higher education should -be penalized for so doing. I submit that the hon. member for Labelle, so far as I have ever been able to judge, is absolutely right on the matter. I have thought of it many times myself, -although I have never spoken of it publicly before, and I hope the minister will even at this stage in connection with this resolution accept the recommendation that has been made by the hon. member for Labelle, and so make it easier for ambitious parents to give their children a higher education.

While I -agree with the last three speakers, the people I am most concerned about are those who do not have an income sufficient to pay am income tax. I have read in the papers -and heard it said in the House that farmers are not paying any income tax. It is obvious why they are not; they are not getting the income on which to pay -the tax. One of the hon. members for Toronto last night repeated the figures he had quoted in the House before in an attempt to prove that Toronto and Montreal are paying nearly all the -taxation, and that -the prairie provinces are paying little or nothing. But there is one fact he has not taken into consideration, and that is that the farmers of western Canada, and I presume tMs also applies to the farmers of Ontario, Quebec, and the maritime provinces, buy hundreds of millions of dollars worth of goods manufactured
Income War Tax Act

in Toronto and Montreal, and added to the price of these goods are -the taxes the manufacturers pay. Naturally ait the ports of entry the customs receipts will roll up high, but these receipts are -simply added to the cost of the goods when they are distributed throughout the country. I say again that I am particularly concerned with these people who have not suffioienit -income on which to pay income tax. It seems to me it is an economic law, when you reduce the income tax, that you either put more taxes on those people, or you lose the opportunity of reducing other taxes, -and I think it is absolutely unfair that there should be a drastic reduction in these taxes, without there being at least a corresponding reduction in the taxes paid by the ordinary people.

Following
the war came responsibilities and obligations which necessitated new forms of taxation. Some of those forms of taxation have rightly been referred to as "nuisance taxes". I trust the time is not far distant when all such will be eliminated. I believe of all the forms of taxation that we adopted the most logical and reasonable was the income tax properly graded. I do not know how much will be lost to the revenue of Canada by this proposed reduction of ten per cent all round, but I will venture to say that the total amount of reduction in the revenue caused by this cut of ten per cent will remain in the pockets of those who are well able to pay that money towards the revenue for the running expenses of the country. This cut of ten per cent in my judgment is a step in the wrong direction. I believe the minister and the government would have been well advised, if, instead of making a cut of ten per cent in the income tax, they had made a further reduction in the sales tax. That reduction would have reached every person to a certain extent. There is absolutely no question about that. There can be no disputing the fact that this reduction of ten per cent does not relieve in the smallest fraction the poor people of the Dominion of Canada. They get no relief whatever from it. The only persons who do and who can get any relief from this reduction of ten per cent are those who are best able to contribute to the revenues of the country and who, because of their personal wealth and influence, ought to contribute. They have a bigger interest than the mere individual who has nothing. There are other forms of taxation which might be imposed by the Minister of Finance to take the place of this one.

I think there is one tax he might impose which would perhaps be received with genera approbation throughout the country. He might put a fair tax upon bachelors.

For instance the hon.
member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott).

There would be a great joy in contemplating such a tax and in seeing whom it would hit. Apart from joking, I wish to place myself on record as saying that I believe this proposed reduction of ten per cent all round in the income tax is a step in the wrong direction, and that reductions might be made in other taxes which would be far more in the interest of those who need reductions.

I should like to endorse the position taken by my hon. friend from Labelle. The hon. member for Frontenac has proposed a tax on bachelors. It seems to me that that would be no more ridiculous than it would be to put a tax, as we do, upon families. It would seem to be quite in keeping that the man who has a large income and no family responsibilities should be taxed more heavily than the man who has a family and who is in every way contributing definitely to the national wealth of the country. But at present we are taxing that man most heavily. I do not know that I can say anything more than has been well said by the hon. member for Labelle. We all recognize that this reduction of ten per cent is a very uneven reduction. Ten per cent may be a comparatively small thing for the man with a small income, but a very heavy reduction for the man with a larger income. Therefore, I beg to move:
That the resolution be amended by inserting after the word "tax" in the second line the words "on incomes under $10,000".

As one of the two who
would be subject to the tax as proposed by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards)-
How about the member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail)?

Three, the Prime Minister, the member for Southeast Grey and myself. I might observe that my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) has overlooked, I think-I submit, at least-the discussion that took place last year. When the income tax was graded as it was last year, there was no provision made to overcome double taxation and I am sure that

Income War Tax Act
a student of economics, such as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, will admit that double taxation is always bad. The taxation of last year imposed upon those who received dividends from companies a double taxation, the dividends being taxed nine per cent in the possession of the company, and in the hands of its shareholders-at rates varying from ten to fifty per cent. This merely remedies the injustice then done. I daresay it is within the memory of the members of this House that their late Minister of Customs said he realized and felt the extent of that unfairness, but that it could not be dealt with at that time, and I am quite certain that the Minister of Finance has been endeavouring to ascertain what percentage of reduction would make a fair adjustment of the difficulty of double taxation. You have no justification for double taxation. For instance, if my hon. friend from East Calgary invests in a company whose net income is $5,000 per annum, that company pays a tax of $450 to the exchequer, being nine per cent of his income, and the money that is left to be divided among the shareholders is thereby lessened by $450 and becomes $4,550 instead of $5,000. Under the existing law that $4,550 is taxed to its full extent, without making any allowance for the fact that in the hands of the company it has already paid nine per cent, and this measure-a tardy measure of justice to those who pay upon the dividend *-is endeavouring-it does not do it amply, it does not come near doing it-to place it upon some basis of fairness or justice. That is the position, and I am satisfied that my hon. friend who comes from my own province and those who do not come from that province, who sit to the left, desire to be fair and just. To make money is not a crime. It is not an offence to honestly toil and get the recompense for it. Toil is not an offence, and never should be an offence in any country, time or place, and the state depends largely on the revenues it can collect, so far as income tax is concerned, from those who, by their enterprise, by their ability, their perseverence, their energy, and their hard work, have been able to accumulate incomes from which the tax can be collected. I am sure that my friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) who spoke a few moments ago will say that he desires to be fair and just to all men. Then if money in the hands of a company is taxed, why should you have double taxation imposed upon it? I put that case to the House last year. The Minister of Finance said that it was worthy of consideration In one instance I pointed out that
money was taxed three times, and the minister said that the difficulty must be overcome. This deduction of ten per cent is merely an endeavour to adjust the taxation so as to prevent money being taxed twice. In England and in all other countries where income tax is collected it is imposed on the principle that money shall not be taxed twice for income tax purposes. This is an endeavour on the part of the minister to carry into effect the suggestion made by the late Minister of Customs himself.
May I go a step further and deal with the matter touched on by the hon. member for Labelle, which I deem of very considerable importance? Ten days ago I heard the case of a gentleman in receipt of a small professional income who has three sons at the university. He and his wife are denying themselves actual necessaries in their endeavour to give their children a chance in life. I do submit to the minister that the exemption should be extended to cover such a case. I agree heartily with the observations made by the hon. member for Labelle and the hon. member for Quebec East. The fact that there are twelve cases of $200 exemption has nothing to do with the matter at all. Where the family revenue is being diminished by reason of the effort made to support a child, whether he be eighteen or twenty years of age in order that that child may be the better able to serve the state, is something that should find recognition on the part of the minister, and I do hope that it is not yet too late for him to take action. When I talked to that gentleman the other day I made up my mind that at the first opportunity I would again urge the minister, as the hon. member for Labelle has so well done, that this exemption should extend to the time while the children are being fitted by their fathers and mothers to become useful citizens of the state. I am sure that to carry the exemption from eighteen up to twenty-one will not involve the sacrifice of much revenue. No one suggests that it should be extended beyond the age of twenty-one, although we all know that the man who sends his boy to a medical school has to support him until he is twenty-five or twenty-six years of age, for during the intervening holidays he is unable to earn any money as he usually goes into a hospital where he gets nothing more than his board. I think the matter is of such importance to the state and to the welfare of families that the suggestions made by the hon. members for Labelle and the county of Quebec as well as by the hon. member for Winnipeg should
Income War Tax Act

receive the hearty support of the House. Let it not be regarded as a contentious political matter. Let us deal with it as something that affects the state as a whole and therefore commends itself to the judgment of every hon. member whether Liberal or Conservative or affiliated with any of the other groups.

I am opposed to any further reduction in the income tax. I do not think for one moment that the sacrifice of the man who is striving to send three boys to university is to be compared with the sacrifice of the fathers and mothers who are struggling to give their children decent food and clothing. One is almost afraid to mention the name of mother here since men preen themselves so much on having large families.
Oh, oh.

I am deeply angered- not for myself, but for the sake of motherhood. This is a masculine House, so masculine that sometimes I resent it from the very depths of my soul. The size of the family is not something for men to boast of. No woman should be asked to bear very large families. It is the men and women who have moderate families and who try to give them decent food and clothing and some education on very slender incomes that I represent here and that I am concerned with. I must take exception to the statement made by the man who has just taken his seat-whom I respect very much personally-that people of great wealth are necessarily good citizens. Very often they are anti-social in all their tendencies and actions, and they are the people responsible for conditions that make it impossible for many boys and girls to ever get a university education. They are the people who will benefit by a reduction in the income tax. So I stand in my place once more to say that I oppose any reduction of the income tax with all my strength. Supposing all our boys and girls go to university and become doctors and lawyers, under heaven what kind of country would we have 1 Sometimes the intellectual snobbishness of people who have received a university training makes me thankful that I have never been able to attend university, much as I have wanted to. If a boy has reached twenty-six or twenty-seven years of age, and has never supported himself, he will not be as good a citizen as if he had at least assisted his parents part of the time in maintaining him. Therefore I repeat, we should not further reduce the income tax. We must have revenue, and if

we do not take it from the people who are able to pay we will have to take it in increasing measure from the people who are not able to pay.

speechtext: I am quoting the same authority as that which I relied on in connection with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Labelle.

May I point out
that if this amendment is adopted, instead of decreasing it will increase the revenues of the country?

speechtext: To that extent it interferes with the scope of the resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I submit that this is an altogether new type of ruling. We have had the rule invoked in the past that a private member is not competent to introduce a resolution which would lessen the national revenues; but it has always been held that it is open to a private member to cut down estimates or to do anything else that would not reduce the revenues of the country. In this particular case the purpose of the amendment is to increase the revenue. If such a ruling as this is to prevail, why, we may as well leave this cpmmittee for it will be absolutely useless to remain here. I challenge the ruling of the chair.

Mr. Chairman, while I
have not consulted the authorities for some years, I still recall some of the rulings of old, and having received within the past two hours advice contradictory to your ruling, I am beginning to ask myself if the rules are to be interpreted according to the convenience of the government or not. I notice that Bourinot is quite clear on this point. For many years he was the respected Clerk of this House, and I think he is just as good an authority as any other that can be cited. I have noticed that at times Bourinot is invoked when his opinion coincides with the interests of the govern-

Income War Tax Act
ment, but otherwise he is ignored. But even May contains a precedent that I think is applicable to the amendment that I proposed. Let me read it.
The principle, that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a minister of the crown, unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of parliament; nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
In support of the last sentence May quotes this precedent:
On the 14th March, 1844, Mr. Howard Elphin-stone proposed a committee of the whole House to consider the Stamp Acts, with the view of imposing the same amount of probate duty on real estate as was paid on personal property.
There we have a very different case. Suppose we had proposed to extend the sales tax upon certain merchandise not already taxed, we should be increasing the area of imposition within the meaning of this opinion. Or suppose we proposed to extend the income tax to certain incomes not already taxed; that, again, would come under this rule. Let us now take our dear friend Bourinot:
If the government approve of any plan of taxation suggested by a private member, it is the constitutional course for them to propose it themselves in the committee of ways and means. This was done in the English House in the ease of a resolution to extend the probate duty upon property above the value of one million. If the government object, that a motion imposing a tax is not required by the exigencies of the public service, the member offering it should at once withdraw it. All the authorities go to show that, when the government have formally submitted to the House the question for the revision of customs and excise duties-*

speechtext:
I would not like the House or the country to be left with the impression, which some of us seem to have this afternoon, that this government have not made any concessions to those who have dependents When the income tax was first introduced I was a member of this parliament and my recollection is that the exemption was $200 for dependents of eighteen years of age and under. This government increased that exemption to $300 and later we increased it to $500. In addition we increased the exemption to the individual so that a married person had an exemption of $3,000 and if there were four children in the family the total exemption would be and is $5,000 to-day. Therefore, if a married man with a family of four children has an income of $5,000 he has no income tax to pay.
In that connection may I give a comparison between the federal government, the different provincial governments that have income taxation and the United States where they have income taxtion? It is true that the exemption under the United States federal act is $3,500 for a married person, but their exemption for dependents is only $400, while ours is $500. The Ontario government have given notice of some changes recently, but they are not applicable on this year's income, and according to our records, in Ontario, for married persons the exemption is only $2,000 and for dependents, $400. In Manitoba the exemption is $2,000 with an exemption for dependents of $300.
Mr. R1CKMAN: The province of Ontario does not collect income tax. The municipalities do so.

While the employees constituted about 73 per cent of the taxpayers, they paid not quite 24J per cent. The merchants paid almost 12 per cent; the manufacturers, 28 per cent, and all others, 30 per cent. The agrarians paid about one-half of one per cent. It is interesting in that connection to remind hon. gentle-ment what I said a few days ago, namely, that the corporations have also paid a considerable amount in taxes and that is not limited to one province. I have already placed that on record.
Some person during the debate suggested that many people were dodging taxes through coupon bonds. That is perfectly true and we know it, but the difficulty is to reach those tax-dodgers. If you put a tax on the coupons, you cannot put a tax on the man who is dodging or trying to dodge taxes without penalizing the honest man as well, because you must tax all coupons. According to the present legislation coupons up to $10 are exempt, so that it is pretty hard to reach that class. My hon. friend is quite right; we know there are people who are dodging some taxes, but, generally speaking, they are paying fairly well.
Just one word in regard to the so-called wealthy individuals who are exempt from this income tax. I think I pointed out to the House during the budget debate that very strong pressure had been brought to bear upon the government from people throughout Canada representing hospitals and other institutions, that we should make exemptions for those who contributed towards hospitals. The ten per cent reduction on the income tax was given as a concession towards that application, and also as a concession, as was represented by the hon. member for West Calgary, the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett), to those who complained that there was double taxation in the legislation of last year. To that extent we have reduced it. But to come back to those who contribute to hospitals, there is at present in Montreal a united campaign being carried on for all their
hospitals. The other day there was brought to my attention the case of a gentleman- and I suppose there are many others-who had contributed $150,000 to this hospital campaign. This sort of thing is going on throughout Canada. These hospitals are maintained not only for the wealthy and other city people who are able to pay, but for those who are not able to pay. It is therefore a little unreasonable always to attack that class of individuals.
I do not want to delay my own legislation; but to come to the observations of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), the exMinister of Finance, and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion), who have urged us to make this further exemption in regard to those who are attending schools or colleges,
I do not know where we are going to reach the limit. We must have revenue from some sources, and the government must have money to carry on and administer the affairs of the country, and to pay the interest on the war debt. I was not very much impressed with the argument of selecting certain persons who were attending college. I was somewhat inclined towards the view expressed by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) that there are other people in this country who deserve consideration. But this appeals to me in the observations of the hon. member for Labelle, that after all, under the law, a Canadian is only legally responsible when he reaches the age of twenty-one years. I will admit, as was stated by the hon. member for Fort William, that as regards some professional men who are sending their children on to higher colleges, we come in under the law and tax them a little more perhaps when the young man or woman is going on to college in order to be equipped to become either a doctor or a lawyer, if you will, I think we have about all the lawyers we can get along with in this House now. I have had an experience of some years in connection with the public schools of our country, and I think people are going into the teaching profession just a little bit too young. I think it might be in the interests of the country if they attended college just a little longer. I have read the record of what my former colleague the Minister of Customs said last year, and while he was very careful and did not make any direct commitment, there was an inference that the government would give consideration to this matter, and so my hon. friend from Labelle will be glad to know that I propose now, Mr. Chairman, to move this amendment.

I have not anything
particular to oppose in this amendment, although on general principles I am opposed to class legislation; I do not think it is right. I think we are on the wrong track when we give special privileges to certain classes of individuals. But what I rose to impress on the minister was this: He has not justified, at least to my mind, his action in taxing gifts to hospitals, and such like. I would like to remind him of the fact that there is hardly a hospital in the country that pays its way, and of the further fact that the people who can pay to go to a hospital are taxed far beyond the actual cost of nursing and medical attention in the hospital. These institutions are run primarily for the benefit of the poor. The nurses in these institutions get practically nothing but their board and lodging and their uniforms, and the medical men and surgeons give their time and their services practically for nothing. That is certainly true with regard to the ward patients. Now the Minister of Finance comes along and instead of relieving these hospitals which are financially embarrassed, he taxes the donations that are made to them. I submit that there is no justification for any such action, which is bound to be reflected in the workings of these institutions. It is going to affect charitable donations to these institutions, which are veiy much in need of help to-day. If these hospitals are to be maintained, they must have the means to carry on, and I submit that this legislation is bad, and it is bound to be reflected in the carrying on of the work of these institutions. I believe the minister should have a better reason than he has given the committee yet for maintaining this tax.

If I gathered the hon.
member's remarks aright, he says that the hospitals are carried on mostly in the interests of the so-called poor people, and that the rich largely contribute out of their means for the maintenance of these hospitals for the benefit of the poor. We in this comer of the House believe and have maintained that the so-called poor man has just as much right to health and the best medical attention as any other citizen of Canada. That is his birthright. We have also maintained in times past, and we do now, that a part of his birthright is a common school education provided out of the taxes upon the community. No doubt in days gone by when schools were not public, philanthropic people gave out of their purse* to maintain private schools and give

the poor an education. But we maintain that the poor people have a perfect right to health and the best medical attention irrespective of their financial condition. My hon. friend's remarks remind me of the statement that was made by a certain gentleman that the Lord created the poor in order that the rich should shower upon them their philanthropy. W'e dissent from that, and I maintain that the day will come when the hospitals will be tax-maintained, and when every man will have the right to the best medical attention without being called poor.

I do not know what
relevance these remarks have to my argument. I am talking of things as they exist to-day. There is no doubt at all that the poor people are being given practically free treatment in the hospitals to-day, and nobody is complaining about that. What I am saying is that these institutions must have financial support, and when people give donations to these hospitals the minister comes along and taxes those donations. I maintain that he has no right to any part of that money.

I do not know what the
hon. gentleman is getting at. He has not shown how much private individuals contribute to the upkeep of hospitals. I can speak with a little knowledge of what is taking place in Winnipeg. Practically all the hospitals in Winnipeg are maintained out of taxes on the community, and I believe that applies to most of the cities in western Canada. Only a very small percentage of the amount of upkeep is contributed by men inclined to give to these institutions. In the case of a poor person who is unable to pay, the municipality is responsible for the amount to the hospital. I believe the very same thing applies in most of the provinces of Canada. I do not believe that five per cent of the amount required for the upkeep of the hospitals is contributed by private individuals in western Canada, and in Winnipeg the facts are exactly as I have stated.

I can also speak with a
little knowledge of Winnipeg, for I lived there at one time. I say that the municipal tax does not cover the nursing and medical attention. It possibly covers the board bill, and that is about all.

For a number of years I was on the board of the General hospital in the city of Winnipeg, and also on the city council, which had to deal with this question. I know the number of appeals that the hospitals make in the city of Winnipeg. Only a couple of weeks ago the city granted an amount in the

neighbourhood of $20,000 to make up the deficit on one year's operation of the General hospital. The municipal hospitals of Winnipeg, which take care of tubercular casesiSome hon. MEMBERS:	Order.

-are maintained entirely out of the taxes levied on the people of the city of Winnipeg, and if my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario had become a little better acquainted with the workings of the hospitals in Winnipeg he would not have made the statement he has made about the extent of philanthropic donations to these institutions. There may be some cities where large grants have been made, but generally speaking, the maintenance of these hospitals comes from the revenue derived from general taxation by the municipalities.

I desire to make a protest against any proposal to exempt from income tax any gifts of wealthy people to hospitals or bo universities, particularly to the universities. Hospitals should be maintained by the municipalities. I think that is almost ' invariably the practice in western Canada. We have hospitals in our rural districts which are maintained by the municipalities. The universities should be maintained by the state and Should not be dependent in any degree upon private subscriptions. It is the duty of the.state to educate our young. Universities should be open to our boys and girls at as low a fee aa possible.
I would not support the amendment with any degree of enthusiasm. I have had to earn my own living since I was sixteen years of age. Many of those boys going to universities would be benefited if they had to go out and earn* the money to enable them to go through the university. I think it might be just as valuable to them in after life as the training they receive in the university itself. Although I am not going to oppose the amendment, possibly the minister would have been well advised to have left it out of the resolution altogether. I hope the time will come-it may be a long time coming-When boys and girls in the keen age, having put in four or five years either on the farm or in the factory, and having a good record from their employers, will be given a chance to go to a university at a cost which they can afford to pay out of the earnings they have made during those years.
hon. members of the House, I have been through a university, and I know that a vast number of the boys and girls put themselves through the universities. I have a boy attending university, as many of us in this House have. A great many of these boys are doing as we did in former days, endeavouring to put themselves through, and instead of getting up and finding fault with the boys and girls who are attending the the universities we should commend them for doing the very thing which will fit them to become good citizens. speakerposition: stagedirection
