subtopic: MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGIAN BAY CANAL COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the happy if somewhat unusual position of being in agreement, with the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). As they have put it, the question is simply whether this House will support the principle of public ownership of public utilities or will sanction the transfer of public utilities to private interests.
I take it that the appropriate time to deal with such a matter as that now before the House is on the second reading of the bill. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie), who is entitled to great consideration when he enunciates points of procedure, has put very clearly before the House the position which the House may and should take on the second reading of a bill such as this. Not only is he entitled to receive the greatest attention, but he is supported by the greatest authority having .to do with parliamentary procedure. More than that, what the leader of the opposition has said and what May in his work says will appeal to this House on another ground even more strongly, and that is that it is common sense; it is the sort of deliverance which will appeal to the wayfaring man as showing the only proper and right course to take.
My friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) cited the case of divorce bills, an unhappy illustration I should think for his side of the question. Of course when we pass the second reading of divorce bills we accept the principle of divorce; it was accepted a long time ago, and whether or not he who votes in favour of the second reading of a divorce bill believes in divorce, he certainly does sanction the approval long ago given to the granting of divorces by this House. The bill then goes to committee, where it is decided whether the standard set up in regard to that matter has been met in that particular bill, but no one would think for a moment that in committee on a divorce
bill that bill should be thrown out because the committee did not approve of the principle of granting divorces.
If we are determined not to give these public rights to private interests, why send the matter to a committee? That would be simply a gesture and' a waste of time, the matter having already been decided by the House. If on the other hand you are ready to grant these public rights to private interests, then by all means send the bill to a committee, because there you can settle the details and terms of the surrender. It would seem certain that if a bill is sent to a committee you adopt the principle of the bill, and how anyone can arrive at any other conclusion or make any sense of an opposite view is not understandable. So I say that this House is perfectly within its rights and is doing the proper thing in fighting out on the second reading of this bill the broad principle contained therein.
As the debate has proceeded and as the various arguments' have been advanced on both sides of the House it becomes more apparent that the line of division between the supporters of public ownership and those who would give public utilities to private interests runs down the centre of the aisle of this House. I have to go back only to the other day when my friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) prevented the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) from making a speech on this very matter. He did it with all the urbanity possible, and possibly had in his mind at the time those words by Lewis Carroll:
"I weep for you," the Walrus said;
"I deeply sympathize.
With sobs and tears he sorted out
Those of the largest size,
Holding his pocket-handkerchief
Before his streaming eyes.
That indication came from that quarter; another came from the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) and then we come to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. McPherson), both bringing specious arguments directed mainly against the province of Ontario and its public utilities, but showing underneath them all that while they were struggling hard to find an excuse they felt in their own hearts that they were doing wrong, and that they were striking a blow against a principle which they have advocated throughout their constituencies. I fancy, Mr. Speaker, that the hustings of Portage la Prairie resounded with declarations in favour of public ownership during the last election campaign; I can imagine that the halls of Marquette re-echoed
Georgian Bay Canal Company

with the same sentiment, and that in the wide open spaces of those constituencies now represented by my Liberal-Progressive friends the air was filled with the determination of these candidates who now sit in the House to uphold this great principle at all costs. Well, the hustings and the halls are waiting; the wide open spaces are still there, and there remains only the home-coming of these gentlemen, to make some explanation of why, on the first opportunity of striking a blow for a principle they had advocated, they were recreant to their promise.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his remarks last night said that the Minister of Railways had removed a good deal of the camouflage which had surrounded this bill. If I may be allowed to say so, Mr. Speaker, I think that is exactly what he did not do; in my humble opinion the Minister of Railways devoted his attention to laying on a particularly thick coat of camouflage. He was debating the amendment before the House, and with the comparatively insignificant omission of any reference whatever to the subject under debate, he made a very good campaign speech. He is not in the House, but I would like to say to him very kindly that during the course of that address it seemed to me that he missed most deplorably the town hall audience which is so admirable a target for such an address. The Minister of Railways wants this bill to go to committee; why? So that the whole question may be before the House. What whole question? Mr. Speaker, the question forsooth of the fight between certain interests known as the Sifton and the Holt interests; that, he said was the bone of contention. I cannot think he is on solid ground there; what business is it of members of this House how Sifton and Holt get on? What have we to do with the gang warfare of private concerns like that? For all we care they may both suffer from their quarrels, the fate of Kilkenny cats. We are here to decide a question which has nothing whatever to do with Sifton or Holt; it is the broad general question of whether we are to control for the people the public utilities of this country.
The Minister of Railways wants the bill to go to committee; why? So that he may commence an expose of some alleged wrongdoing on the part of the late government. If there has been any wrong-doing, by all means bring it out. If the Carillon order in council contains matters that require explanations, let those explanations be made. There are ways of doing this. Let it come up in the proper way; let the House have the

whole matter before it, and if there was any wrong-doing on the part of the previous Conservative government, let it be brought out. No one will welcome that more than those who sit on this side of the House. We do not believe from what we hear there is anything in the one-sided story which the Minister of Railways has given to us; but be that as it may, I still say that it has no relevancy whatever to the discussion in which we are engaged at the present moment. May I suggest in all kindness that the reason why the Minister of Railways, speaking for the government, wants this bill to go to the committee, is that he may, by calling witnesses for this and that, by raking up scandals and old political scores, endeavour to evolve political material for the next occasion on which he may hope to use it.
The government has deliberately, so he says, brought up this matter. If that be so, I wonder at their bringing it up by way of a private bill advanced by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier). If they want to make the fight and bring the whole matter up for discussion and settlement by the House, let them come at it direct and unafraid and not shelter their attack behind a private bill introduced by a private member. The speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite seek to divert the attention of the House from the real issue. It is all very well to speak of the northern part of Ontario and its power problem, to talk of the Gatineau, to hold out fears of this and that; but the purpose underlying all the addresses made on the opposite side of the House is manifest to everyone who is here, namely, to divert our attention from the matter that is really before the House for discussion. The Minister of Railways made an admirable speech of its kind; but, as I say, it had absolutely nothing to do with the matter under discussion. If we analyze it in its application to what we are discussing, and if it is an argument at all, it is that sort of argument which is variously described from the "tu quoque" of the erudite down along the line to the equally understandable colloquialism of "so's your old man." In other words, it is that sort of argument that finds its ultimate conclusion in this and in this only: "If we are doing wrong, we are excused because you also did wrong."
I shall not pause to consider longer the red herring which has Ibeqn attempted to be drawn across the trail, the red herring of the Carillon order in council. But this side of the House is, I am assured, ready and willing to meet any discussion on that matter when it is brought up for discussion. I mistake very much if the most thorough search

Georgian Bay Canal Company
amongst the proceedings taken by the late government will show that there is any deep-dyed villain in the plot; that there has been any plan which has a bearing directly or indirectly upon the question of the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal. Be that as it may, if the government be sincere in what the Minister of Railways has said, let it open up the matter as soon and as widely as it can.
The government may have a suspicious mind; it seems to have imagination. A theory is propounded that strikes one as being the sort of stuff that dreams are made on. The same suspicion seems to have been aroused in the mind of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen); but strangely enough that suspicion did not first find expression in this House. It found expression first in an interview granted by one of the Siftons, I think Mr. Harry Sifton, and quoted in this House not long ago, when he said that the whole secret of the opposition to the bill lay in the fact that the St. James street interests, or the "crowd", or whatever the words were, had tried to run Canada and, failing in that, they were now endeavouring to run the House of Commons. That is the genesis of the whole argument. That is where it sprang from. If it has been adopted by the government or by the Liberal Progressives, so much the worse. Any member who is swayed by such clap-trap as that is welcome to the sensation.
Are we to renew this charter which is now thirty-four years of age, with nothing as yet accomplished, nothing attempted to be done? Is it to be forever rejuvenescent? Are we to be met every year or every two or three years, or whatever the terms of the extension may be, by the Siftons holding for ransom one of the most valuable rights that Canada can give away. This is the time and this is the place when we should strike a blow that will deliver us from this threat now and for all time to come.
A great deal has been made by the interests who are supporting this bill of an amendment which was introduced into a renewal act dated in 1912, whereby the price of power was to be fixed before sale by the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. The literature of parties supporting this bill, sent out from time to time, has made a great deal of capital of the statement that Sir Adam Beck agreed that the bill might go through provided only that this clause were inserted. It is within the memory of man that that is not the case; it is not true. Sir Adam Beck was here in 1912 fighting this bill as hard as he knew how. He was overcome; the bill was going through and he saved what he could. He accepted the clause which the committee
offered to put in, fixing the price of power by a reference to the Board of Railway Commissioners; but to say that he consented to the bill then or at any time before or after, is an absolute untruth. He did not consent to the bill; he opposed it to the best of his ability, and as the result of his fight he only managed to have that clause, a futile clause,
I may say, inserted in the bill.
Can we consider that as some sort of clause which will help us in the sale of power? What is to be the price of power? To begin with, the Board of Railway Commissioners has no facilities whatever for determining what shall be the price of power, and the price of power generated in the Ottawa river will be the price not only of the power itself but of the canals and other works that go to make up that scheme. The board has announced the policy and it has adhered to it in case after case that on all common stock of companies, like the Bell Telephone Company, which handle public utilities, there shall be an 8 per cent dividend and over and above that a 2 per cent allowance on capital stock for profit. That means a 10 per cent return on all the company's stock, watered as it may be. You would have something that people would find absolutely impossible to overcome in purchasing power. The owners would have along the Ottawa river a monopoly that could not be met by any development which the Ontario hydro has. What the traffiic will bear will govern the price.
I believe Quebec is just as much interested in having its industries along the Ottawa river maintained as is Ontario, and the rights of these two peoples, on either side of that great interprovincial stream with its unlimited water-powers, are to be sacrificed to the demand of politicians, whether associated with the government or not, who seek to get this great heritage for their private and personal ends.
This is ostensibly a canal, Mr. Speaker. Very well, then; if it is a canal, why have it built by private enterprise? The day of the toll gate is past. We can remember roads than ran through Ontario, and hon. gentlemen will no doubt remember them in every other province, where you had to pay at a gate every now and then for the privilege of travelling over that road. That is a thing of the past, and yet this bill proposes to -make a great national waterway, something of infinitely greater importance than a road, subject to tolls at the instance of a private corporation. But we need not concern ourselves muich in regard to the canal or the canalization part of this bill. The Minister of Railways and Canals who spoke
Georgian Bay Canal Company

on behalf of the government the other evening said that this is not a canal scheme but a power scheme, and the whole question is as to who shall have the control of this vast reservoir of power. Then are we here, I ask once more, to determine a fight between two rival interests, or are we to determine a fight between private enterprise on the one side, and on the other the control by the people of this Dominion of their own great natural resources in order that they may develop them for the public good?
The maritime provinces have grievances, Mr. Speaker. Out in the western provinces the question of the natural resources being returned to the provincial government has become an active issue, and we hear that claims are being made in British Columbia for the return of what they consider themselves entitled to. Here we in the central provinces are asking at the same time for something of the same sort. We do not claim anything positive. It has been interesting, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the discussion upon the bill before the House respecting the Georgian bay canal. We in northern Ontario are vitally interested in this matter, because a waterway from the Atlantic to the head of the lakes that would pass by our front door would mean something to northern Ontario. It would mean a great deal to the district of East Algoma, which I have the honour to represent in this House.
Listening to the discussion as it has proceeded I could not help wondering whether we were afraid that the canal would not be built, or whether the fear wras that the canal might be built. Frankly I almost think the apprehension is that the canal might possibly be built. I am convinced it would be of great advantage to the Dominion of Canada. It could not help but prove of wonderful advantage to northern Ontario to have this great waterway pass along just where it is needed in order to benefit that section of the country. During the past number of years that district has made rapid progress. For a long time it has been asking for hydro development and it is greatly interested in this scheme. It is true that in old Ontario the hydro-electric has made wonderful progress because of the fact that behind the project are strong municipalities that are able to give their bonds under the guarantee of the government of Ontario. That is the system on which the Hydro Electric Power Commission is able to function in Ontario.
The discussion so far, rather than following along the line of the canal, has drifted into a discussion of power development; I wish, therefore, to speak for a few minutes on that phase of the question. Northern Ontario has not. had the advantage of hydro-electric development. I think I am correct in saying -and someone will correct me if I am wrong -that there has been only one power development in northern Ontario by the Hydro Electric Power Commission, and that development would not be possible were it not for the cities of Fort William and Port Arthur. Northern Ontario is a new country and it has not been possible for the hydro-electric commission to develop those powers, owing to the lack of municipalities strong enough to get



Georgian Bay Canal Company
behind the scheme; and so the developments in northern Ontario have been made by private concerns and private capital. Were it not for the private capital expended in northern Ontario that country would not be developed to the extent that it is to-day. Where is the government, where is the parliament, that would pass estimates for large, untried developments when the public does not know whether or not they would be a success? Private enterprise has gone into northern Ontario and made that country what it is to-day, and, Sir, this House is not in a position to vote 3100,000,000 to go on with the project. I feel quite sure that unless this development is undertaken by private enterprise) the Georgian bay canal will not be built. I do not know whether or not the Georgian bay canal is feasible. I do not know whether or not this is the right company to develop that project, but I do say that this bill should go to committee, and in the committee we ought to have an opportunity of gathering the facts and hearing the different people who are interested in it so that we may form an opinion and decide whether or not the bill should be passed.
It is said that this development ought to be carried, on by the government, and that is quite true; that would be the proper course if the government were in a position to go ahead with it. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is not going to be very long until this House will have to decide upon another development, namely, the development of the St. Lawrence. I am satisfied that the government will not be prepared to find the money for both of them in the near future.
We fin northern Ontario, I repeat, .are vitally interested in the bill which is now before the House. Judging from the discussion which we have had in this House it would seem to be the

I find myself, Mr. Speaker, very much in the plight of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) when he said last night that he intended to speak upon this question without very much preparation. However, having lived in the city of Toronto, and being familiar with the great benefits that the Hydro Electric Power Commission has conferred upon Ontario, I feel that this is an opportunity to declare the faith that is in me, a faith that I believe is held pretty generally throughout the country by all who know what the development of hydro-electric power under public ownership has meant for this province.
But what troubles me is that we are dealing with a bill that, mark you, does not mention a single word about power. This bill which we have so long discussed is a pure sham. I-n support of that statement I appeal to the recollection of the House as to what the Minister of Railways said last night when he jumped into this fight. He stated: Now, we all acknowledge that the bone of contention with respect to this bill is which of two private interests shall control the Carillon power. The first bill incorporating this company was passed thirty-four years ago when our predecessors had not the slightest thought of the development of the water-powers of this country. What do we find to-day? By a fluke and a side issue what never was in the minds of the original incorporators is now, according to the Minister of Railways, the chief consideration upon which hon. members are asked to decide whether or not this bill shall be given second reading.
It is plain that what is involved in this bill is not the construction of a canal but the acquisition and development of very valuable water-powers that the promoters-and I have no doubt there are more than two parties-would like to secure, and therefore I say it is time for us to pause before we take further action. I am satisfied that nothing in the nature of a canal is contemplated by those who are seeking a renewal of this charter. It it were possible to test the real opinion of hon. members, I feel certain that everyone in whatever quarter of the House he sits would acknowledge that there is not the slightest chance of a dipper of water being turned into any canal that 32649-7SJ
will ever be built under this legislation. But we find northern Ontario declaring: Oh, the north needs a canal. I am confident that it does, and I would welcome the construction of a canal for the benefit of the people there who might have occasion to use it with profit. But the bill is so framed that there can be no possible prospect of a canal ever being built under it.
This measure, Mr. Speaker, reminds me of a bill that was before this House in 1925 to sanction the Petersen contract. That contract was signed by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce on behalf of the Dominion. The preamble of the bill with a great flourish set out that it was important in the interests of Canada that the Dominion should control ocean freight rates. But having read that contract, it was apparent to me, as it must have been to anyone who read it intelligently, that instead of giving to the Dominion the control of ocean freight rates, it placed that control absolutely in the lap of the late Sir William Petersen. I desire to make some
few observations with respect to this department generally. For a few weeks-it is a pity it was not longer-I was acting minister of this department, which is manned by a number of very efficient, hard-working and not over-paid officials. In the main they are endeavouring to do a great service to this country, but the real fact is that a very great proportion of this amount asked for is money absolutely lost. Why? Because in the first place in each province there is at least one university undertaking to do some of this work; then again the province is endeavouring to undertake some part of it, and there is also the Research Council which desires to take its share of this obligation. Unless and until there is coordination of the efforts of the provinces, through the universities and through the departments of government, the Research Council and this Dominion, I am
bound to say that the federal Department of Mines becomes more or less the fifth wheel on the coach. What is the sum total of the real services rendered by this department to the Dominion of Canada during the past twelve months? Just sit down and consider that question. We spent over half a million dollars in this department; what is the sum total of ita contribution to the wealth of the nation?
The great problem now confronting us is how most readily to create new wealth, and mining offers a very ready means to that end. Last year we created new wealth through mining to the extent of something over S242,-000,000. If my hon. friend asks them what particular branch of their industry they think this has benefited, they might answer in a very offhand way: Well, not anything of a very definite character, but scientific research is so important in regard to many of our problems that are giving us trouble that we want investigation carried on in the laboratories in connection with them. I might mention the extraction from jack pine of the resinous content, the handling of the cottonwoods, the high grade treatment of pulp manufactured even from our best grade spruce. These are all problems that can be worked out in the laboratory. I mention these in passing to show the importance of this wrork.
The hon. member for Fort William has touched upon another important problem. If my hon. friend would ask me what the United States, who are spending millions of dollars instead of thousands, and rightfully so, have accomplished in securing a better process for the treatment of their low grade ores, I would say that they have made no greater progress than we have. Our chemists are working on this problem, just as they are on oil problems and on the treatment of the gases which my hon. friend mentions. Three years ago a company was given a lease in Alberta for the manufacture of carbon black. They never went into business. Why? For the simple reason that I would not give them a lease in the areas contiguous to railways, but only in the areas where gas was escaping anyway. That was in the Pelican rapids field, a long distance from the railways. My hon. friend knows that the very rapid development in the southern states brought into the market tremendous volumes of gas which was turned into carbon black, with a consequent reduction in price to about six cents a pound, so that this company could not hope to exist.
So far as all these problems are concerned, may I say to my hon. friend that a very real effort is being made to prevent overlapping by the universities, the National Research Council, and government departments. I have on my desk in my office a list of the problems that the council have announced they are now investigating. They are not all in Canada, but the council is watching" every one of these problems. I might add

I just want to make clear one thing. I suggest that a particular branch of that work be taken by this department, leaving to the universities another branch, and to the provinces another branch, rather than that an effort be made by the three to undertake this work jointly; and the same with respect to research. With respect to the paper industry and what has been done as a gift, surely my hon. friend was not here the other day when Dean Hibbert of McGill made his address, a most amazingly interesting address it was too, with respect to the utilization of scientific research in industry. But as perhaps my hon. friend knows, the chair that Dean Hibbert occupies was established through the benevolence of the late Mrs. Eddy, who left $200,000 to the university for that purpose. That is how the chair came into being, and the paper industry put up $350,000 for the purpose of providing a building for McGill.
The hon. gentleman knows that I share his views with respect to the value of research. All I was endeavouring to make clear to him was this: Could we not make it certain that the university, the province, the Research Council, and this department should each pursue definite lines of action so as to prevent the possibility of duplication? I think the minister has endeavoured to do that, but it has not always been done, I regret to say. If he exercises firmer control over that matter we should get better results.
I know what research means. All one has to do to appreciate its value is to remember what the Germans have done with respect to research. Take, for instance, the specific known as 606, which has been so valuable in disease. It represented 606 different experiments, any one of them taking sometimes months to carry out, with measurements and everything of that sort; hence the name, 306. That gives one some idea of what research means. On the [DOT]other hand, I think it is desirable that one body should be pursuing one definite course 
of experimental work and another body another line, in order that there might not be duplication, and in order that there might be a correlation of their effort when they finish their experiments.

I think my hon. friend from West Calgary is right in his contention that there should be probably more cooperation than there has been, only, between not the universities and this department but also between the universities and the provincial departments. I have a great deal of sympathy with the minister in regard to the work that has been done by the Mines branch. I remember during the past year some friends of mine basing their explorations in a new mining section of this country absolutely upon reports made years before by some mines branch-I do not know whether it was of this government or of a provincial government. But these men actually went out and searched for minerals basing their explorations entirely on this report, made many years previously, and they found veins in the Woman lake and Red lake country which promise to be immensely rich. I have a very great deal of respect for the work done by the Mines branch, and I agree with the minister that its value cannot be estimated except over a period of years.
I wish to come back for a moment to the iron question. It is of so much importance that this government might well consider the advisability of adopting the report made in 1923, I think it was, by the committee appointed by the Drury government. In that report, as I mentioned in my remarks on the budget, it was recommended that the provincial and federal governments combine in a bounty system to develop the iron ore resources of this country. I pointed out at that time that Mr. Corliss, of the Mond Nickel Company, had quoted American geological survey experts as saying that we had 9,000,000,000 tons of low grade iron ore, 35 per cent ore, in this country, which could be developed if a plan were evolved for that purpose. Obviously 35 per cent ore cannot compete with 45 per cent ore without assistance of some kind from either the Dominion or the provincial government. I remember in 1924 putting a question on the order paper addressed to the present minister, then Minister of Mines, asking him what was being done in regard to that report, and he said that it was under consideration. That was three years ago.' The Minister of Finance told us this afternoon that several matters were still

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
under consideration, and I presume this iron ore report is still under consideration-or perhaps it has passed out of consideration altogether. The minister might be well advised, however, even with his more or less pronounced free trade views, to consider on behalf of his government the possibility of adopting that report and cooperating with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The province of Quebec, in view of the immense deposits of titanic iron ore discovered around Chicoutimi, put through a resolution in 1925 advocating a bounty system. If the minister would come forward with a bounty system for developing our iron ore deposits that would prove a success, as I believe it would, its value to this whole country would be such that nothing could pry this government loose from its seats for many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nothing can anyway.

The minister said that last year, but we pried him loose for a few months at least, and then somehow they sneaked in again. But I would be willing for the good of my country to see the government come forward with a proposition to cooperate with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and other provinces in which there are iron ore deposits, and if the results were attained which I believe could reasonably be anticipated, this government might easily stay in power for a long time, and deservedly so. I think the minister might well give that suggestion much more consideration than he has in the past on behalf of the country as a whole, because there is no doubt that the iron and steel industry is the basic element -in the commercial progress of any country. The progress of every country which has made important commercial advancement has 'been based on a foundation of the development of iron and steel. I could give a list of the countries, but I have done it in the past and I shall not do it to-night. Of course coking coal enters into the development of iron and steel, and we have I think the second greatest deposits of coal in the 'world. We have the iron ores, and we have large quantities of the limestone which is necessary to this development. I hope, therefore, that the minister will seriously consider the remarks I have made in reference to this matter and will take some action in order to keep this moribund government in power for a few years.
I wish to commend the government for this vote, but I also wish to condemn it for its action in another regard-
Hear, hear.

Someone says "hear, hear". I quite agree with the minister that there is no department of the government that offers such possibilities for scientific research as this one. But I want to bring home to them the fact that the action they have taken is hopelessly inadequate to the requirements of the country. We have an advisory council on scientific and industrial research, but it has been practically starved for years. When the Department of Health came into existence some years ago a special condition stipulated was that there was to be a department of scientific research, but such a department has not yet been formed. We are leaving this matter, which is after all one of federal concern, tu universities and to private individuals and companies, and any result we have got has been practically the result of private research. In the realm of medicine the discovery of insulin was made by Doctor Banting, who, we are told, spent practically his last dollar before he succeeded. He got no help from any government and is not getting it to-day. We are turning these matters over to universities, which I think is a mistake. Of course the universities should take them up but after all the object of universities is to train men in fundamental science, which is a different thing. This department should be fostered and maintained by the government not only in this branch, but in every branch. As we look over the countries of the world and see what they have done, and as we look over the possibilities of scientific research in Canada, I say we have starved the department. I hope the government, the Finance minister and the Minister of the Interior will loosen up their exchequer a little' bit and give this department the money it ought to have. With the great natural resources we have in this country, the possibilities of multiplying our national wealth not only ten or twenty but a hundredfold are immense. I repeat that I hope the government will give these departments a little better financial support in the future than they have in the past. I make these comments because I desire to say a word on behalf of two great departments, that of scientific and industrial research and that of health, which have been in existence for some years but which have been poverty-, stricken to such a degree that their efforts have been almost futile. I heartily support the minister in this vote, but I say the government are not living up to their duties as a government in this matter, and I can only hope that in future they will do better.

friend says that this ought all to be done at Ottawa. In the United States, after careful thought, instead of establishing a central bureau of mines the government have scattered thirteen stations throughout the country, all doing extensive work. I do think that to a limited, perhaps even to an extended, degree medical research may be very helpful, but I am very anxious that there shall not be any overlapping, because in the long run it means an added burden upon the shoulders of our tax payers. I am confident that one of the most important things we can do is to establish in Ottawa a central organization to coordinate scientific work all over the Dominion. speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
On every
occasion since I have been a member of the government I have stressed the importance of scientific research, and I am bound to say that with the exception of an odd member here and there not very much interest has been evinced in the subject. Apparently we must first bring home to the people a realization of the value of scientific research in industry, both manufacturing and agricultural, before we shall be able to get the money required for this work. We need two or three million dollars to make a beginning, and the expenditure will run into a very considerable amount to meet the requirements of scientific research even to a limited degree.

I submit that in the first place the services have been starved, and in the second place that there has been no directing force. I think we should have in Ottawa a central force which would form the nucleus *of a scientific industrial research council. It might be all right for the universities to look after this work, but I do not think that is their function. The universities should train men in scientific research so that they may be available to the government. I agree with the minister that we cannot look for results immediately, probably we would not get any for years, but in the process of solving various problems unexpected discoveries might be made. In fact that is how all the great discoveries of science have been made: scientists have been looking for one thing and have discovered another. These discoveries have been of immense value to the country, but there should be a central directing force in Ottawa to whom all departments might look for guidance. I do not say that this body should necessarily do the work, but certainly there should be some central authority to assign various subjects to the different departments, or the universities, if you will.

Mr. MaeLEAN (Prince): I wish to place myself on record in support of the minister's request for a larger vote. I had the pleasure a few days ago of listening to Doctor Hibbert of McGill university who delivered an eloquent lecture bearing on this subject. Doctor Hibbert occupies the Eddy chair in the university in question, and speaking in the Chateau Laurier he gave a most instructive address on Borderland Sciences, in which he showed the correlation of one- science to another. It was one of the finest addresses to which one could possibly listen, and it revealed the extensive work which may be done in the line of scientific research. He told us what the universities were doing, and pointed out vividly what the Dominion and provincial governments should do in this direction. Not only in relation to the subject of medicine, to which he referred, did he reveal some of the most startling facts, but as regards the treatment of products in everyday use he gave some arresting information. There is a great field for development not only in minerals but in every other line. I had a conversation the other day with Doctor Gussow of the Dominion experimental farm

here in connection with the growing of potatoes, which is a matter of considerable importance to my own province. I would not have said anything on the subject but for the suggestion made by an hon. member that the Department of Mines should send out prospectors. In my opinion, speaking from experience, the very best work that could be done for prospectors generally is being done by the geological parties which are sent out by the federal and provincial governments. The geological surveys which they make are eagerly looked forward to by all prospectors year by year. The prospectors know where these survey parties operate and they try to get the newest geological maps available for the various areas. Every prospector to-day realizes the great value to them of these geological surveys, and you cannot meet one on the trail who is not equipped with the latest map of the particular country he is prospecting. The map discloses the geological characteristics of the country, with marks indicating what veins have been found, together with information relating to the assays that have been made. Practically all of the geologists sent out by the Department of Mines to-day are excellent prospectors as well as scientific men, and the work they are doing is certainly wonderful. I wish to make a few remarks, but not of a critical kind, because I ' realize that the department has been doing good work under somewhat restricted circumstances. I would refer particularly to northern Manitoba, where nature has been very lavish but at the same time very perverse in the intricate manner in which the elements have been mixed together. The question of copper mining in northern Manitoba is a standing challenge to the scientific minds of Canada, and I am curious to know just how far the department has been addressing itself to these problems which loom very large to us in that part of Canada. I think it will not be denied that there we have some of the finest copper deposits on this continent, but these are awaiting the discoveries of our scientists. I understand that with regard to the well-known Flin-Flon property, an American firm has been experimenting there for some two or three years; I think it somewhat of a humiliation to us as Canadians that the solution of these immensely important problems should] be left to the enterprise of scientists outside our borders, but so it has been in this regard. I do not know just what progress they are making along these lines, but I wonder if the department knows; I wonder if there is any cooperation and if our Department of Mines has been keeping track of the work undertaken by this private enterprise. If that has not been the case, perhaps a little criticism might be expected. It seems to me that a process which is fraught with such tremendous importance to the northern part of Manitoba and to Canada as a whole should be followed carefully by this department. Personally I am not much concerned about geological exploration; I think perhaps that has gone almost as far as

It seems inevitable that if oil development is going to be permitted in Turner valley, we must expect a considerable wastage of gas for some time to come.
Then Dr. Allan goes on to say, according to this report:
Dr. Allan, however, emphasizes the point that adequate regulations must be enforced to prevent unnecessary wastage of gas in drilling wells and cites a bad example, "Due to lack of supervision", he says, "wells were drilled in the Peace river district and from at least two of these water and gas have been flowing for many years. They are now 'running wild' and the chances are that this uncontrolled water has probably ruined the possibility of getting oil from at least the higher horizons in that district."	[DOT]
Attention i| also drawn to the very important fact that the Dominion government regulations apply only to Dominion lands, and these regulations do not apply to free-hold lands which include those lands held privately by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and by the Hudson's Bay Company.
Any regulation that is made to cover the development of petroleum or natural gas in Alberta should apply to all lands, irrespective of ownership.
The reason I am bringing this matter to the attention of the minister and the committee is to ask whether any research work is being carried on by the department looking to the prevention of this wastage, and whether the government are carrying on any investigation as to the possibility of capping new wells *which may be brought in. Probably forty new wells are at present being drilled in that area. If even one-half of these should be brought in during the coming year, there is going to be a heavy flow of gas from them. I have been much interested in the remarks made by many hon. members to-night regarding the development of the mineral resources of Canada. It is quite right that we should develop these resources. The

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
fact, however, is that this natural gas which is being wasted can never be replaced. The minerals as long as they lie in the ground are not at any rate being wasted, but this natural gas is in many cases being burned to get rid of it and wt are wasting a very valuable natural asset. It is important that the department should carry out any investigational work which may appear possible to them looking toward the control of the flow of natural gas from those wells and also towards the utilization of the gas which is now flowing from them, because I understand it has been found impossible to cap some of them. Possibly, if it is not already being done, the department might investigate the cost of producing electric energy from this gas which is now going to waste. It seems to me that it would not cost any more to install internal combustion engines near this gas field and to produce power in that way than to install turbines in hydro-electric power plants. I would be glad if the minister would inform the committee, particularly for the benefit of the people of Alberta, whether any investigational work along this line is being carried on, and also whether they have in mind any way of preventing the wastage of gas especially from new wells which may be brought in.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
About a
year ago, we employed an English engineer, probably one of the most outstanding men in his profession, for the very purpose of preventing what has happened on one or two occasions, if not more-and I know of at least three-where wells, when they struck the heavy flow, blew everything to pieces, twisting their casings and running wild for weeks at a time, the flow of gas from them being wasted. If my hon. friend will remember, about eighteen months ago I came in for some severe criticism when w'e were insisting on cementing the pipe in rock when wells were being drilled in heavy gas strata. The result was that when gas was struck we could cap the well, if need be, and preserve that gas, shut it off completely. That has not been the case where we do not control the property. My hon. friend has mentioned the fact that many of those lands are privately owned and the federal government has no jurisdiction in that case. The control of property and civil rights is primarily a provincial matter. But where the lands are owned by the federal government and leased by them, we have absolute control and we are seeing that proper precautions are taken to prevent that heavy flow of gas from throwing the casing out of the well and causing a great deal of trouble. In
the north I do not know how that gas can be shut off, because there is no rock strata and this wastage has been going on there for a number of years. Wherever there is a rock strata we have shut off the flow at considerable expense to the federal government. In addition we have Mr. Elworthy working continuously on the development of processes for the utilization of the gas, and any of the small municipalities such as High River might very well utilize that gas for the purpose of securing power for the generation of electricity. There is no necessity of research for that; all they have to do is to pipe the gas to a given point and generate electricity from that gas.
As regards federal property we are very much exercised about this matter and we are giving it a great deal of consideration and careful thought. For that reason we have employed this gentleman, who has had a wide experience in drilling for oils and in the proper care of the drilling process to preserve this great natural product if it is found.

Is it possible to procure

speechtext: No, that was not the reason.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I can
give my hon. friend the explanation. When Mr. Meighen's government resigned and the present administration assumed office in October last, Mr. Meighen continued as leader of the opposition until the time my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Guthrie) was chosen leader of the opposition. Unfortunately immediately after we came into office, Mr. Meighen was informed that no salary cheques could be paid to him as leader of the opposition, or to his secretaries and that he was not entitled further to the use of the frank. When I learned of this, I expressed considerable indignation and said I thought it was quite wrong. It seemed to me that the House would not desire the leader of the opposition to be treated with discourtesy of the kind. I was informed that there was no legal authority to pay Mr. Meighen as leader of the opposition, that the law required that to be recognized as the leader of the opposition he must be a member of parliament, and at the time Mr. Meighen had not a seat. I discussed the matter with Mr. Meighen personally and said I would take the responsibility of seeing that matters were properly adjusted. It was then that Mr. Meighen informed me that he had received no salary as leader of the opposition for the period here mentioned though he had acted as such during that time. I said if that were the case I thought it was equally a mistake; that if he was entitled to the salary he should receive it, and that I would ask the House to vote it, this I now desire to do.

I am glad we have received this explanation because we in this group were wondering why it was included in the supplementary estimates when the salary of the leader of the opposition is provided for in the House of Commons Act. I would like to go a little further than (that and point out that there is another circumstance which the Prime Minister evidently has not taken into consideration. The government of which the Prime Minister is now head took office on December 29, 1921, if I am not mistaken, and after the general election prior to that Mr. Meighen did not have a seat in the House and had to wait until such time as a seat was opened to him dn order to enter the House. Another circumstance which we must remember is the fact that the party led by Mr. Meighen was not the second largest party in the House and could not claim in any way to be the official opposition. The Conservative party had something like fifty-one members whereas the Progressive party had about sixty-three, and it was not determined until March 6 or 7 which of those two groups would form the opposition. Under no circumstances could Mr. Meighen and the Conservative party claim the opposition benches until such time as the Progressive group had made a decision as to whether or not they would form the opposition. I think it was on March 6 that the Progressive group decided not to become the official opposition, and that information was transmitted not only to the Prime Minister but to Mr. Meighen as well, as leader of the Conservative party. Under the circumstances Mr. Meighen never was the deader of the official oppposition at that particular time. I am not objecting to the amount of the vote, but 1 do think at this late hour of the day and in view of these circumstances it is pretty small to include that sum of money in the estimates.
